title: ISACA CISM
subtitle: Certified Information Security Manager exam prep
source: Structured on ISACA's CISM Exam Content Outline (in force until 2 November 2026), with the 3 November 2026 update. Independent study material, not affiliated with ISACA
description: All four CISM domains subtopic by subtopic, the manager mindset and exam technique, the new architecture content from November 2026, formulas and recovery terms, CISM-style quizzes and a practice exam.

chapters.title: About CISM and the exam
chapters.summary: What CISM is, exam format, domains, eligibility, maintenance and the November 2026 update.

blocks.text: The **Certified Information Security Manager (CISM)** credential from ISACA certifies that you can design, manage and oversee an enterprise information security programme. ISACA has awarded it since 2002, and more than 111,000 professionals have earned it.

CISM is a **management** certification. It tests whether you can align security with business goals, manage risk, run a security programme and lead incident management. It does not test deep technical skills such as configuring firewalls or writing exploits.

rows: Managing and governing an information security programme
Broad security knowledge across 8 domains, more technical

blocks.title: Why it matters for a leadership path
blocks.text: CISM is one of the certifications most often listed in CISO and security leadership job descriptions, because it proves you can speak the language of governance, risk and business value, not only technology.

rows: 150 multiple-choice questions, one correct answer out of four
Scaled score from 200 to 800; 450 or higher passes
PSI test centres or remote online proctoring
US$575 for ISACA members, US$760 for non-members
Book up to 90 days ahead; appointments available as early as 48 hours after payment
Waiting period between attempts (check ISACA's current retake policy)

blocks.title: A scaled score is not a percentage
blocks.text: 450 does not mean 56% correct. ISACA converts raw scores to a 200-800 scale so that different exam versions are comparable. Aim for 75% or better on good practice questions before you book.

sections.title: The four domains (outline in force until 2 November 2026)

blocks.text: Each part lists subtopics. This book follows them one by one, so every subtopic in the official outline has its own section.

blocks.title: Where the marks are
blocks.text: Domains 3 and 4 carry 63% of the exam. Governance is only 17%, but its thinking (business alignment, senior management accountability, risk-based decisions) is how you pick the right answer in every domain.
ISACA announced on 10 September 2026 an updated CISM exam content outline. Updated preparation materials launched on 1 September 2026, and the updated exam is available from **3 November 2026**.

items: **New content areas:** enterprise architecture and information security architecture.
**More emphasis:** information security strategy and program development.
**Unchanged:** 150 questions, 4 hours, 450 on a 200-800 scale to pass.

blocks.title: Which outline applies to you
blocks.text: If you sit the exam on or before 2 November 2026, the current outline applies. From 3 November, study the new outline too: read the Architecture chapter in this book and check ISACA's Exam Content Outline page for the full list of new subtopics, which third-party sources had not reproduced at the time this book was written.
Becoming certified

items: **Pass the exam.**

**Experience:** five years of information security work experience, including at least three years of information security management across three or more of the CISM domains, gained within the 10 years before applying or within five years after passing.

**Substitutions:** up to two years of the general experience can be waived, for example for holding CISA or CISSP, or for a relevant postgraduate degree. The three years of security management experience can't be waived. Check ISACA's current substitution rules.
**Apply within five years** of passing, and pay the US$50 application fee.
**Agree to the ISACA Code of Professional Ethics** and the CPE policy.

blocks.text: Staying certified

rows: At least 20 hours each year and 120 hours over each three-year period
US$45 per year for members, US$85 for non-members
A random sample of holders must provide evidence of reported CPE; failing the audit can lead to revocation

blocks.text: Every CISM holder agrees to the Code. In summary, members commit to:

items: Support effective governance and management of enterprise information systems and technology, including security, by implementing appropriate standards and procedures.
Perform duties with objectivity, due diligence and professional care.
Serve stakeholders' interests lawfully, with high standards of conduct and character, and not discredit the profession.
Maintain the privacy and confidentiality of information obtained in their work, unless disclosure is legally required.
Maintain competency and only undertake work they can reasonably complete with the necessary skills.
Inform appropriate parties of the results of work performed, disclosing all significant facts known to them.
Support the professional education of stakeholders in understanding governance, security and risk.

blocks.title: Ethics in questions
blocks.text: When a scenario involves pressure to hide a finding or overstate compliance, the answer that reports facts to the appropriate party through proper channels is almost always right.

sections.title: What ISACA expects you to do: the 37 tasks

blocks.text: The outline lists 37 supporting tasks that describe the job. Paraphrased and grouped:

rows: Identify influences on strategy; build strategy, governance framework and policies; write business cases; gain senior leadership commitment; define responsibilities; report programme effectiveness and metrics

Run the programme in line with strategy and business functions; maintain processes, resources and documentation; run awareness; build security into organisational processes and contracts; monitor third parties; define metrics; classify assets; identify compliance requirements

Oversee risk identification, assessment and treatment; oversee vulnerability and threat analysis; select risk responses within risk appetite; judge whether controls are adequate; integrate risk into business and IT processes; monitor for changes; report risk to stakeholders

Maintain the incident response plan aligned with BCP and DRP; classify incidents; detect them promptly; investigate and document lawfully; handle containment, notification, escalation, eradication and recovery; staff and train teams; communicate internally and externally; test plans; run post-incident reviews

items: Read the **CISM mindset** chapter first. It changes how you read every question.
Work through the domain chapters in order. Governance first, because it underpins everything else.
Take each chapter quiz. Read the explanation even when you get it right: the reasoning is what the exam tests.
Use the flashcards for terms and formulas (ALE, RTO, RPO, KRI and so on).
Finish with the **Final review** and the **Practice exam** chapters.
Pair this book with ISACA's official Review Manual and question database (QAE) matching your exam outline.

quiz.q: How many questions are on the CISM exam, and how long is it?
What is the passing score?
quiz.explain: A scaled score of 450 or more passes.

quiz.q: Which domain carries the most weight?
Which content areas are added from 3 November 2026?
options: Enterprise architecture and information security architecture
quiz.explain: Two new areas: enterprise architecture and information security architecture.

quiz.q: How many CPE hours must a CISM holder earn?
quiz.explain: At least 20 annually and 120 per three-year cycle.

chapters.title: The CISM mindset and exam technique
chapters.summary: Think like a security manager: business first, risk-based, governance-led. How to read and answer questions.

sections.title: Think like a manager, not a technician

blocks.text: Most wrong answers in CISM are technically correct but **wrong for a manager**. The exam rewards the answer a senior security manager would choose in a real organisation.

rows: Install a tool to fix it
Understand the business impact and risk first, then decide
Follow the policy, the incident plan or the agreed escalation path
The business (risk or asset owner) decides; security advises and informs
Protection proportionate to risk and within risk appetite
Find the root cause and fix the process
Report to the party with authority to act (often senior management or the risk owner)

blocks.title: The golden thread
blocks.text: Business objectives, then risk, then controls. When unsure, choose the answer that connects security to business objectives or to risk-informed decisions by the right owner.

items: **Senior management is accountable.** Boards and executives own information security governance and risk decisions. The security manager enables and advises.
**Risk owners accept risk, not security.** The security manager makes sure the owner understands the risk.
**Business alignment comes first.** A strategy, programme or control that doesn't support business objectives is the wrong answer.
**Policy before procedure, strategy before tactics.** Governance artefacts come before tools.
**Assess before you act.** Understand the current state, impact or root cause before choosing a solution.
**Follow the plan.** In incidents, the incident response plan and escalation paths come before improvisation.
**Cost-effective, proportionate controls.** Spending more than the risk is worth is wrong.
**Prevention and detection before correction** where it's practical, but recovery capability is mandatory.

rows: The step that must come before all others
Usually assess, understand, identify, or consult the plan
The option that achieves the goal most completely and appropriately
Several answers may work; pick the one aligned to business and risk
The factor with the greatest influence on success
Often senior management support, business alignment or risk
Think about why something exists, not side benefits
The most probable cause or outcome
Choose the common, realistic answer, not the exotic one
Look for impact on the business or loss of accountability

blocks.title: Eliminate first
blocks.text: Remove answers that are technical point fixes, bypass governance, or assign accountability to the wrong person. You are often left with two; choose the one closer to business objectives and risk.

items: Read the last sentence first: what exactly is asked (FIRST, BEST, MOST)?
Identify your role in the scenario. You are almost always the information security manager.
Identify the stage: governance, risk, programme or incident. Where in the process are we?
Predict the answer before reading the options.
Eliminate options that are too technical, too late in the process, or outside your authority.
Choose the option that is most business-aligned and risk-based.
Don't overthink. If two answers look right, ask which one a CISO would present to the board.

blocks.title: Worked question
blocks.text: **An employee reports that a laptop containing customer data was stolen. What should the information security manager do FIRST?** A) Notify customers. B) Wipe the laptop remotely. C) Follow the incident response plan to assess the incident. D) Report it to the police. **Answer: C.** Notification and wiping may follow, but the first step is to invoke the plan and assess (was the disk encrypted? what data?).

rows: Mindset, exam format, Domain 1 (governance and strategy)
Domain 2 (risk assessment and response), including quantitative calculations
Domain 3 (programme development and management), the largest domain
Domain 4 (readiness and operations), including BIA and recovery terms
Architecture chapter (essential if sitting on or after 3 November 2026)
Practice questions under timed conditions; review every wrong answer

blocks.title: The practice question trap
blocks.text: Memorising answers from a question bank doesn't transfer to the real exam. For each question, explain in one sentence why each wrong option is wrong. That builds the judgement the exam tests.

quiz.q: A business unit wants to launch a product with a known security weakness. Who should decide whether to accept the risk?
options: The business owner, with senior management as appropriate
quiz.explain: Risk acceptance belongs to the owner with authority; security advises.

quiz.q: Which answer style is MOST often correct in CISM?
options: Align to business objectives and manage risk to acceptable levels
Escalate every issue to law enforcement
quiz.explain: Business alignment and risk-based decisions are the core of CISM.

quiz.q: A question asks what to do FIRST. Which type of answer is usually right?
Who is ultimately accountable for information security governance?
quiz.explain: Governance accountability sits with the board and executive management.

quiz.q: Which is the BEST reason for a security control?
options: It reduces risk to an acceptable level cost-effectively and supports business objectives

chapters.title: Domain 1A: Enterprise governance
chapters.summary: Governance fundamentals, organisational culture, legal and regulatory requirements, structures, roles and responsibilities.

blocks.text: Ensures that stakeholder needs are evaluated to set agreed objectives, that direction is set through prioritisation and decision-making, and that performance and compliance are monitored. The board and executive management own it.
Plans, builds, runs and monitors activities in line with the direction set by governance to achieve objectives.

The part of corporate governance that provides strategic direction for security activities, makes sure objectives are achieved, risk is managed appropriately, resources are used responsibly and the programme's success is monitored.
The six outcomes of information security governance

rows: Security supports business strategy and objectives
Security strategy traced to business goals; business leaders on the steering committee
Risk is managed to an acceptable level within risk appetite
Approved appetite statement, risk register, treatment plans
Security investments deliver value and are cost-effective
Business cases, benefits tracking, standardised controls
Knowledge, people and infrastructure are used efficiently
Shared services, documented processes, skills plans
Metrics show whether objectives are being met
Assurance functions (audit, risk, compliance, legal, HR, physical security) work together
Integrated assurance map, shared findings tracking

blocks.title: Remember the six
blocks.text: Strategic alignment, risk management, value delivery, resource optimisation, performance measurement, assurance integration. Questions often describe a symptom (e.g. duplicate audits) and ask which outcome is missing (assurance integration).
Culture is the set of shared values, beliefs and behaviours that shapes how people actually act, whatever the policy says. A security manager can't change culture by decree but can influence it.

items: **Risk culture:** how willing people are to take risk, report problems and challenge unsafe decisions.
**Security culture:** whether people see security as part of their job or as someone else's obstacle.
**Tone at the top:** visible behaviour of leaders (using MFA, attending exercises, funding security) sets norms.
**Culture differs by region and unit:** a group-wide approach must allow for local norms, languages and regulations.

rows: Formal policies accepted; slower change; escalation paths matter
Guardrails and automation beat long policies; security must not block speed
Invest time in stakeholder buy-in before launching initiatives

blocks.title: Exam angle
blocks.text: If a control keeps being bypassed, the best answer is rarely "enforce harder". Look for the answer that addresses culture: awareness, business involvement, simplifying the control, or leadership support.
The security manager must identify every external obligation that affects information security and make sure it is addressed in strategy, policy and controls.

rows: EU GDPR, Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017, Saudi PDPL, UAE PDPL, South Africa POPIA
Central bank cyber directives, insurance regulators, telecom regulators, health regulators, critical infrastructure rules
PCI DSS for card data, SWIFT Customer Security Programme for banks
Customer security clauses, data processing agreements, SLAs, cyber insurance conditions
Data localisation, transfer restrictions, export controls
E-discovery, legal hold, evidence requirements, breach notification deadlines

items: Keep a **compliance register** with owners, and monitor for changes.
Map requirements to controls once and reuse evidence ("test once, satisfy many").
Involve **legal counsel** to interpret laws; the security manager does not give legal opinions.
Where requirements conflict (e.g. retention vs deletion), escalate to legal and senior management.

blocks.title: Compliance is a floor, not the goal
blocks.text: CISM treats compliance as a minimum. The best answer usually manages risk to the organisation's appetite, which may require more than the regulation demands.

rows: Sets direction and risk appetite; oversees security as a business risk; ultimately accountable
Implements governance; provides resources; owns enterprise risk decisions
Cross-functional group of senior business and IT leaders that prioritises, approves and oversees security initiatives
Develops and runs the programme; advises on risk; reports on posture; coordinates incident management
Own processes and associated risk; approve controls and accept residual risk
Accountable for classifying data and approving access; usually senior business managers
Implement and operate protections (often IT) on behalf of owners
Independent assurance to the board on control effectiveness
Risk management, compliance, legal, HR, privacy (DPO)
Partner functions for enterprise risk, obligations, people and privacy

blocks.text: Reporting lines

The CISO's reporting line affects independence. Reporting to the CEO, COO, CRO or directly to a board committee gives more independence than reporting inside IT, where a CIO may face a conflict between delivery speed and security.
Useful tools

items: **RACI matrix** (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for key processes.
**Segregation of duties** so no single person can complete a sensitive transaction end to end.
**Security champions** in business units to extend reach.

blocks.title: Accountability can't be delegated
blocks.text: Responsibility can be delegated; accountability cannot. If asked who is accountable for protecting customer data, the answer is the data owner or senior management, not the custodian or security team.

quiz.q: Which is the PRIMARY goal of information security governance?
options: Providing strategic direction so security supports business objectives and risk is managed
quiz.explain: Governance aligns security with business objectives and ensures risk is managed.

quiz.q: Separate audit, risk and compliance teams each test the same controls with different findings. Which governance outcome is weakest?
Who should classify customer data?
quiz.explain: The data owner is accountable for classification.

quiz.q: What is the BEST way to gain acceptance of security in a fast-moving digital business?
options: Security guardrails that enable delivery and involve business leaders

quiz.q: A new data protection law applies to the organisation. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Work with legal to understand the requirements and assess current gaps
quiz.explain: Understand obligations with legal, then assess gaps.

quiz.q: Why is a CISO reporting line outside IT often preferred?
options: Greater independence and fewer conflicts of interest

chapters.title: Domain 1B: Information security strategy
chapters.summary: Developing strategy, governance frameworks and standards, and strategic planning with budgets and business cases.

blocks.text: A security strategy describes how security will support the organisation's objectives over a period (typically three to five years). It links business goals to a desired security state and a roadmap.

items: **Understand business strategy and objectives** (and what the business is trying to become).
**Identify influences:** threats, regulation, technology changes, culture, stakeholder expectations.
**Define the desired state** (e.g. target maturity, target CSF profile, risk appetite).
**Assess the current state** (maturity assessments, audits, risk assessments).
**Analyse gaps.**
**Build a roadmap** of initiatives, sequenced and resourced.
**Define metrics** to track progress.
**Obtain senior management approval and commitment.**

blocks.text: Constraints on strategy

Strategy must work within constraints such as legal and regulatory requirements, physical constraints, ethics, culture, organisational structure, costs, personnel, resources and capabilities, time, and risk appetite.

blocks.title: The most important input
blocks.text: The MOST important factor in developing a security strategy is the organisation's business objectives (with risk appetite close behind). Answers that start from threats or technology alone are usually wrong.

rows: Governance and management framework for enterprise I&T: 40 objectives in EDM, APO, BAI, DSS, MEA
Governance structure, alignment with enterprise IT, capability assessment
Certifiable ISMS standard with 93 Annex A controls; 27002 gives guidance
Outcome framework: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover

blocks.text: Business Model for Information Security (BMIS)

ISACA's BMIS views security as a system of four elements (**organisation, people, process, technology**) connected by six dynamic interconnections: **governing** (organisation-process), **culture** (organisation-people), **enabling and support** (process-technology), **emergence** (people-process), **human factors** (people-technology) and **architecture** (organisation-technology). A change in one element affects the others.

blocks.title: Frameworks are tools, not goals
blocks.text: The exam favours adapting frameworks to the organisation's context. "Implement every control in the standard" is rarely the best answer.

sections.title: Strategic planning: budgets, resources and business cases

blocks.text: Business case

items: Problem or opportunity in business terms.
Options considered, including doing nothing.
Costs: capital and operating, internal effort, ongoing maintenance.
Benefits: risk reduction, compliance, enabling revenue, efficiency.
Financial measures: ROI, NPV, payback period, return on security investment (ROSI).
Risks of the initiative itself and dependencies.
Alignment to strategy and how success will be measured.

blocks.text: Return on security investment = (risk reduction in money - cost of the control) / cost of the control. Example: ALE falls by $80,000 for a $20,000 control, ROSI = (80,000 - 20,000) / 20,000 = 300%.
Budget and resources

items: Tie budget lines to roadmap initiatives and risks, not to tools.
Separate run costs (operations, licences) from change costs (projects).
Plan people: skills inventory, hiring, training, outsourcing and managed services.
Use maturity models (CMMI or COBIT capability levels 0-5) to express current and target state.

blocks.text: Getting commitment

Senior management commitment is the single most important success factor for a security programme. Gain it by presenting risk and value in business terms, linking initiatives to business objectives, and reporting progress regularly.

blocks.title: Typical question
blocks.text: "What is the MOST effective way to obtain senior management commitment?" Answer: present a business case showing how security supports business objectives and reduces risk. Not: show threat statistics or compliance penalties alone.

rows: High-level statement of management intent and direction
All information must be classified and protected according to its classification
Mandatory requirement that supports a policy
Passwords must be at least 14 characters or use MFA
How to request and approve access in the IAM tool

blocks.title: Policies change slowly
blocks.text: Policies should be technology-neutral and stable. If a question describes a new technology, the answer usually changes a standard or procedure, not the policy.

quiz.q: What is the MOST important input when developing an information security strategy?
Which is the FIRST step in developing a security strategy?
In BMIS, the dynamic interconnection between people and technology is...
quiz.explain: Human factors connects people and technology.

quiz.q: A control costs $25,000 per year and reduces ALE from $120,000 to $40,000. What is the ROSI?
Which document states management's high-level intent?
quiz.explain: Policies express intent; standards make them mandatory and specific.

quiz.q: What is the MOST effective way to gain senior management commitment?
options: Present a business case linking security to business objectives and risk
quiz.explain: Business value and risk in business terms.

chapters.title: Domain 2A: Information security risk assessment
chapters.summary: Risk fundamentals, emerging threats, vulnerability and control deficiency analysis, and risk assessment methods.

rows: Anything of value to the organisation: information, systems, people, reputation
Anything that can cause harm by exploiting a vulnerability (actor or event)
A weakness that can be exploited
How probable it is that a threat will exploit a vulnerability
The consequence to the business if it does
The combination of likelihood and impact of an adverse event
The amount and type of risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of objectives
Acceptable deviation from risk appetite for a specific objective
The maximum risk the organisation can absorb before it fails or can't meet objectives

blocks.text: Risk management frameworks

items: **ISO 31000:** enterprise risk management principles and process.
**ISO/IEC 27005:** information security risk management.
**NIST SP 800-30** (risk assessment), **800-37** (Risk Management Framework), **800-39** (organisation-wide risk).
**COBIT 2019 / COBIT for Risk** and ISACA's **Risk IT** concepts.
**FAIR:** quantitative analysis of loss event frequency and magnitude.
**OCTAVE:** self-directed, asset-focused risk assessment.

blocks.title: Risk is always business risk
blocks.text: Information security risk matters because of its impact on business objectives. When a question asks how to express risk to senior management, choose business impact (money, customers, regulation, operations), not technical severity.

rows: Double extortion (encryption plus data leak) makes backups alone insufficient
Attacks through software updates, MSPs and SaaS platforms bypass your perimeter
Phishing, MFA fatigue, session token theft; identity is the new perimeter
Public storage, excessive permissions, weak control plane security
Deepfake fraud, faster phishing; risks from your own AI use such as data leakage and prompt injection
Legacy devices connected to IT networks; safety impact
Long-term, targeted intrusions; critical infrastructure focus
Malicious or careless employees and contractors
New privacy, AI and cyber resilience laws create compliance risk

items: **Sources:** threat intelligence feeds, national CERTs, ISACs, vendor reports, law enforcement advisories.
**Threat modelling** (e.g. STRIDE, attack trees, MITRE ATT&CK) translates threats into scenarios relevant to your assets.
**Horizon scanning:** review emerging technologies the business plans to adopt.

blocks.title: New technology adoption
blocks.text: When the business wants to adopt a new technology (AI, cloud, IoT), the best first step is a risk assessment of that use case, not an outright ban and not unconditional approval.

items: **Vulnerability identification:** scanning, penetration testing, code review, configuration reviews, audit findings, threat intelligence.
**Control deficiency analysis:** compare required controls (from policy, standards, frameworks) with what is implemented and effective.
**Design vs operating effectiveness:** a control can be well designed but not operate consistently, or operate consistently but be badly designed.
**Root cause:** fix the process that allowed the vulnerability, not just the instance.
**Prioritise** by exploitability, exposure and asset criticality, not raw count.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A scan finds 3,000 vulnerabilities. Analysis shows 80% come from servers built without the hardening standard. The control deficiency is the build process, so the fix is enforcing hardened images in provisioning, not patching servers one by one forever.

rows: Rates likelihood and impact on scales (e.g. low to high), often in a heat map
Subjective; hard to compare with financial decisions
Assigns numeric scores to qualitative scales
Uses monetary values and probabilities (e.g. ALE, FAIR, Monte Carlo)

blocks.text: Quantitative formulas
Asset value (AV) x exposure factor (EF).
Expected number of occurrences per year (e.g. once every 4 years = 0.25).
SLE x ARO.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A customer database is valued at $500,000. A breach would destroy 40% of its value (EF), so SLE = $200,000. It's expected once every 4 years (ARO 0.25), so ALE = $50,000. A control costing $20,000 a year reduces ARO to 0.05: new ALE $10,000. Annual benefit = $50,000 - $10,000 - $20,000 = **$20,000**, so the control is justified.
Process

items: Define scope and context (assets, processes, risk criteria).
Identify risks: assets, threats, vulnerabilities, existing controls.
Analyse likelihood and impact.
Evaluate risk against appetite and criteria to prioritise.
Record in the risk register and hand to risk treatment.

blocks.title: Asset value first
blocks.text: Before assessing risk you must know what assets exist and what they are worth to the business. A question asking what's needed FIRST for a risk assessment often wants asset identification and valuation.

A **risk assessment** asks how likely and harmful events are. A **business impact analysis** (Domain 4) asks how harmful a disruption to each process would be over time, whatever the cause. Together they tell you where to invest in prevention and where in recovery.

rows: What could happen and how likely is it?
What happens to the business if this process stops?
Risk and security management with business owners

quiz.q: Risk that remains after controls are implemented is called...
An asset worth $1,000,000 has an EF of 25% and an ARO of 0.2. What is the ALE?
What should be done FIRST in a risk assessment?
quiz.explain: You need to know what you are protecting and its value.

quiz.q: The business wants to use a public generative AI service. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Assess the risk of the intended use cases
quiz.explain: Assess the risk of the specific use, then decide with the business.

quiz.q: Which is the BEST way to express information security risk to the board?
Which method BEST supports a cost-benefit decision on a control?
quiz.explain: Quantitative results are in monetary terms.

chapters.title: Domain 2B: Information security risk response
chapters.summary: Treatment options, controls, risk and control ownership, and risk monitoring and reporting.

rows: Implement controls to reduce likelihood or impact
Add MFA to reduce account takeover risk
Shift financial impact to a third party
Cyber insurance; outsourcing with contractual liability
Knowingly accept the risk within appetite
Accept risk on a low-value internal system
Stop the activity causing the risk
Decide not to store card data; exit a risky market

items: Choose options by comparing **cost of treatment** with **risk reduction** and appetite.
**Transfer never transfers accountability.** If a cloud provider leaks your customers' data, the regulator still comes to you.
**Acceptance must be formal:** documented, approved by someone with authority, time-limited and reviewed.
Some risks need a combination (e.g. mitigate and insure the residual).

blocks.title: Classic trap
blocks.text: "Risk was transferred to the insurer, so it's no longer our concern." Wrong: insurance covers some financial loss, not reputational damage or legal accountability.

rows: Alternative when the primary control isn't possible
Extra monitoring on a legacy system that can't be patched

blocks.title: Control objective first
blocks.text: Define what the control must achieve (control objective), then choose the control. It keeps choices tied to risk rather than products.

rows: The risk: accountable for deciding the response and accepting residual risk. Usually the business owner of the process or asset
A control: responsible for designing, operating and evidencing it
The process: facilitates assessment, advises, monitors and reports

items: Every risk in the register needs a named owner with authority and budget.
Ownership should sit at the level that can act, not the most junior person available.
When no one accepts ownership, escalate to senior management.

blocks.title: Who accepts risk?
blocks.text: If the question asks who should accept residual risk, pick the business or risk owner (or senior management), never the security manager or IT.
A metric that signals a change in risk exposure, ideally before a loss. Example: percentage of critical systems missing patches beyond SLA.
The central record of risks with owner, rating, treatment, status and review date.

items: **Reassess risk when things change:** new systems, mergers, new regulations, new threats, major incidents, audit findings.
**Report by audience:** board (top risks, trends, appetite breaches), executives (risk by business unit, treatment status), operations (detailed findings).
**Heat maps and trends** show movement; pair them with narrative on what decisions are needed.
**Escalate** risks outside appetite promptly.

blocks.title: Change triggers reassessment
blocks.text: A question describing a merger, new cloud platform or new law usually wants "reassess risk" before any specific control.

items: **Change management:** security impact assessment before approval.
**Project and SDLC:** security requirements at the start, threat modelling, security testing before go-live.
**Procurement:** third-party risk assessment before contract.
**Mergers and acquisitions:** security due diligence before completion.
**Enterprise risk management:** cyber risks reported alongside financial and operational risks using common scales.

blocks.title: Early is cheaper
blocks.text: The best time to address security in a project is the requirements or design phase. Answers that add security at testing or after go-live are rarely BEST.

quiz.q: A company buys cyber insurance for ransomware. Which risk response is this?
quiz.explain: Insurance transfers part of the financial impact, not accountability.

quiz.q: Who should accept residual risk for a customer-facing application?
options: The business owner of the application

quiz.q: Additional monitoring on an unpatchable legacy server is what type of control?
quiz.explain: It compensates for the missing primary control.

quiz.q: The organisation is acquiring a competitor. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Assess the security risks of the acquisition
quiz.explain: Reassess risk when significant change occurs.

quiz.q: Which metric is BEST as a key risk indicator?
options: Percentage of critical systems with overdue patches

quiz.q: When is the BEST time to address security requirements in a new system?
quiz.explain: Early is cheaper and more effective.

chapters.title: Domain 3A: Information security program development
chapters.summary: Programme resources, asset identification and classification, standards and frameworks, policies, and metrics.

blocks.text: The **information security programme** is the set of activities, resources and processes that delivers the security strategy. Strategy says where to go; the programme gets you there and keeps you there.

items: **Programme charter:** mandate, scope, authority, governance and reporting lines, approved by senior management.
**Scope:** business units, geographies, technologies, third parties.
**Roadmap:** initiatives from the strategy, sequenced by risk, dependency and resources.
**Integration:** alignment with IT, HR, legal, procurement, audit, risk and business operations.

rows: Roles and skills, headcount, training, succession, retention, segregation of duties, security champions
Documented, repeatable processes (risk, access, change, vulnerability, incident)
Chosen to meet control objectives; integration and operating cost matter as much as features
Managed security services, consultants, cloud providers; accountability stays internal
Linked to roadmap and risk; run vs change costs

blocks.title: Programme success factor
blocks.text: The MOST important factor for programme success is senior management support, followed by alignment with business objectives. Tools and headcount come after.

items: **Identify assets:** information, applications, infrastructure, cloud services, people and facilities.
**Assign owners** who are accountable for each asset.
**Value assets** by business impact (confidentiality, integrity, availability), not purchase price.
**Classify** using a simple scheme (e.g. Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted).
**Define handling rules** for each level: storage, transmission, sharing, retention and disposal.
**Label and enforce** through tools (labels, DLP, access control).
**Review** classifications periodically and when data changes.

blocks.title: Why classify?
blocks.text: The PRIMARY purpose of classification is to apply protection proportionate to the asset's value and sensitivity. Over-protecting everything wastes money; under-protecting creates risk.

blocks.title: Keep it simple
blocks.text: Three or four levels is usually enough. Complex schemes with seven levels are rarely applied consistently.

sections.title: Industry standards and frameworks for information security

blocks.text: Standards give the programme a proven structure and make it easier to demonstrate compliance to others.

blocks.title: Map once, comply many
blocks.text: Choose one primary control framework and map other obligations to it. Separate programmes for each standard multiply cost and confuse owners.

items: **Policy framework:** one top-level policy approved by the board or executives, supported by topic policies (access, acceptable use, classification, incident, third party, cloud, AI).
**Lifecycle:** draft with stakeholders, approve, communicate, implement, monitor compliance, review at least annually or after major change.
**Exceptions process:** documented request, risk assessment, compensating controls, approval by risk owner, expiry date.
**Enforcement:** technical enforcement where possible; HR disciplinary process for violations.
**Acknowledgement:** staff confirm they have read key policies.

blocks.title: Policy exceptions
blocks.text: If a business unit can't comply with a policy, the best answer is a documented exception with risk acceptance by the appropriate owner and compensating controls, not ignoring it and not immediately changing the policy.

rows: No major incidents affecting customer data this year
Mean time to patch critical vulnerabilities
Number of privileged accounts without MFA
Risk trend vs appetite; progress on strategic roadmap; maturity score
Programme milestones, control coverage, budget use
Patch compliance, alerts handled, scan coverage

items: Good metrics are **SMART**: specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, timely.
Metrics should drive decisions. If no one would act differently based on a metric, drop it.
A **balanced scorecard** can show security across financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives.

blocks.title: Metrics for the board
blocks.text: The BEST metrics for senior management show risk and progress against business objectives. Technical counts (number of blocked attacks, viruses detected) are poor board metrics.

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of information classification?
options: To apply protection proportionate to value and sensitivity

quiz.q: Who should approve the top-level information security policy?
A business unit can't meet a policy requirement for six months. What is the BEST response?
options: Document an exception with risk acceptance, compensating controls and expiry
quiz.explain: Formal exceptions keep risk visible and owned.

quiz.q: Which is a KRI rather than a KPI?
options: Mean time to close service tickets
Number of privileged accounts without MFA

quiz.q: Which metric is MOST useful to the board?
options: Trend of top risks against risk appetite

quiz.q: What is the MOST important factor for security programme success?

chapters.title: Domain 3B: Controls, design to testing
chapters.summary: Control design and selection, implementation and integration, and testing and evaluation.

items: Start from **control objectives** derived from risk and requirements.
Select controls based on **cost-effectiveness**, feasibility, impact on business processes and fit with the architecture.
Apply **defence in depth**: multiple layers so one failure doesn't expose the asset.
Prefer **automated, preventive** controls where practical; add detective and corrective layers.
Consider **people, process and technology** together (BMIS).
Use recognised baselines (e.g. CIS Benchmarks, ISO/IEC 27002, NIST SP 800-53) and tailor them.

rows: Users and systems get only the access they need
Access to information only when required for a role
No one person controls a sensitive process end to end
On failure, the system defaults to a safe state
Never trust by network location; verify each request

blocks.title: Business impact of controls
blocks.text: A control that blocks a critical business process is a bad control, even if it is secure. The best answer balances protection and business operations.

items: **SDLC and DevSecOps:** security requirements, secure coding, testing and gates in pipelines.
**Change and configuration management:** hardened baselines; security review of changes.
**Identity and access management:** joiner-mover-leaver, MFA, privileged access management, access reviews.
**Data protection:** encryption, key management, DLP, backup.
**Network and cloud security:** segmentation, secure cloud configuration, shared responsibility.
**Endpoint security:** EDR, patching, device management.
**Monitoring:** logging, SIEM, SOC processes.
**Physical and environmental security.**

blocks.title: Integration beats islands
blocks.text: Controls work best when built into existing processes (HR onboarding, procurement, change approval) rather than run as separate security steps people can skip.

rows: Owners check their own controls; builds accountability
Assurance to the board on design and operation
ISO 27001 certification, SOC 2 reports, regulatory audits
Prove exploitability and test detection and response

blocks.text: Whether the control, if operated as intended, would achieve its objective.
Whether the control actually works as designed, consistently over time.

blocks.title: Independence matters
blocks.text: The person who designed or operates a control should not be the only one testing it. Questions about assurance usually favour an independent party.

quiz.q: What should drive control selection?
options: Control objectives derived from risk and requirements
quiz.explain: Control objectives come from risk and requirements.

quiz.q: Which principle ensures no single person can create and approve a payment?
A control works when tested once but fails intermittently in practice. What is weak?
quiz.explain: Operating effectiveness is consistency over time.

quiz.q: Who should provide independent assurance on control effectiveness to the board?
A proposed control would stop a critical business process. What should the security manager do?
options: Find an alternative control that meets the objective with acceptable business impact

chapters.title: Domain 3B: Awareness, third parties and reporting
chapters.summary: Awareness and training, management of external services, and programme communications and reporting.

items: **Programme, not event:** onboarding, annual refreshers, ongoing short content, simulations.
**Role-based training** for developers, administrators, executives, finance and HR.
**Tailor** to audience, language and culture; use real examples from the organisation.
**Measure behaviour:** phishing report rates, repeat clickers, incident reporting times, policy violations, not just completion.
**Leadership participation** reinforces importance.

blocks.title: Awareness effectiveness
blocks.text: The BEST indicator that awareness works is a change in behaviour (e.g. more phishing reports, fewer incidents caused by users), not the number of people who completed training.
Providers, suppliers, third parties and **fourth parties** (your suppliers' suppliers) extend your attack surface. The security manager integrates security across the whole relationship lifecycle.

rows: Classify the service by risk; assess security (questionnaires, SOC 2, ISO 27001 certificates, site visits)
Security requirements, right to audit, breach notification timelines, data location, subcontractor controls, SLAs, exit terms, liability
Least-privilege access, secure integration, contacts for incidents
Performance and SLA reviews, reassessment, security ratings, incident reporting, fourth-party changes
Revoke access, return or destroy data with certification, transition support

items: **Cloud shared responsibility:** the provider secures the platform; you secure your data, identities and configuration.
**SOC 2 Type I vs Type II:** Type I assesses design at a point in time; Type II assesses operating effectiveness over a period (usually 6-12 months).
**Concentration risk:** too many critical services with one provider.

blocks.title: Accountability stays with you
blocks.text: Outsourcing a service outsources the work, not the accountability. The BEST protection is security requirements in the contract, verified by ongoing monitoring and the right to audit.

rows: Top risks, appetite breaches, trend, major incidents, decisions required
Programme progress, risk by business unit, resource needs
Risks and actions in their area, their responsibilities
Evidence of compliance and control effectiveness

items: Report **risk and business impact**, not activity counts.
Be honest about gaps; credibility is the security manager's most valuable asset.
Tie every request for budget or decisions to risk and objectives.

blocks.title: Reporting noncompliance
blocks.text: If a significant control failure or noncompliance is found, the information security manager must report it to senior management (or the appropriate owner), even if it is embarrassing to IT or the business.

quiz.q: What is the BEST indicator of an effective awareness programme?
What is the BEST way to ensure a cloud provider protects your data?
options: Include security requirements and right to audit in the contract, and monitor compliance

quiz.q: A SOC 2 Type II report provides assurance on...
options: Design at a point in time
quiz.explain: Type II covers operating effectiveness over time.

quiz.q: Who remains accountable for customer data processed by an outsourced provider?
What should the security manager report to the board?
options: Top risks, trends against appetite, and decisions needed
quiz.explain: Board reporting is about risk and decisions.

chapters.title: Enterprise and security architecture (new from November 2026)
chapters.summary: Enterprise architecture, security architecture frameworks, principles, zero trust and cloud reference architectures.

sections.title: Why architecture joins the CISM outline

blocks.text: ISACA added **enterprise architecture** and **information security architecture** to the CISM outline from 3 November 2026, recognising that security managers must understand the technologies and structures under their oversight. For CISM, the focus is the manager's view: how architecture aligns security with business strategy, how to govern it, and how to use it to make consistent decisions.

blocks.title: Scope check
blocks.text: ISACA's full new subtopic list wasn't publicly reproduced when this book was written. This chapter covers the core concepts a manager is expected to know. Confirm the exact subtopics on ISACA's CISM Exam Content Outline page before your exam.

A structured description of how an organisation's business processes, information, applications and technology fit together, today and in a target state, and a discipline for moving from one to the other.

rows: The Architecture Development Method (ADM): Preliminary; A Architecture Vision; B Business; C Information Systems (data and application); D Technology; E Opportunities and Solutions; F Migration Planning; G Implementation Governance; H Architecture Change Management; with Requirements Management at the centre
A classification matrix: six questions (what, how, where, who, when, why) against six perspectives (from planner to worker)
Managed Enterprise Architecture as a management objective

items: **Baseline and target architectures** mirror the security strategy's current and desired state.
**Architecture principles** (e.g. "data is an asset", "security by design") guide design decisions.
**Architecture governance:** an architecture review board approves designs against standards; security should be a voting member.
**Building blocks and reference models** make approved patterns reusable.

blocks.title: Manager's angle
blocks.text: The best answer usually embeds security in the EA process (security requirements in each ADM phase, security on the architecture board) rather than reviewing designs after they are built.
The design of security controls, services and their relationships across the enterprise, aligned to business requirements and the enterprise architecture.
SABSA
SABSA (Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture) is a business-driven security architecture framework. It works through six layers, each answering what, why, how, who, where and when:

rows: Business requirements, risks and attributes (e.g. available, confidential, compliant)
Security strategy, principles and control objectives

blocks.text: SABSA's **attributes profiling** turns business goals into measurable security attributes, giving traceability from business requirement to control.

blocks.title: Traceability is the point
blocks.text: Whether you use SABSA, TOGAF security guidance or your own method, a good security architecture lets you trace every control back to a business requirement and risk.
**Zero trust** (NIST SP 800-207) assumes no implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is authenticated, authorised and evaluated continuously.

rows: Decides whether to grant access based on policy and signals
Establishes or shuts down the session based on the decision

items: Signals include user identity, device health, location, behaviour and data sensitivity.
Micro-segmentation limits lateral movement.
Identity becomes the primary control plane.
Zero trust is a strategy and a journey, not a product.

blocks.text: Other patterns

items: **Defence in depth** and **segmentation** (zones and conduits in OT).
**Secure access service edge (SASE)**: network and security services delivered from the cloud.
**Cloud reference architectures** and landing zones with built-in guardrails.
**Security as code**: policies and controls in version-controlled templates.

sections.title: Governing architecture as a security manager

items: Define **security architecture principles** approved by governance.
Maintain **reference architectures and patterns** so projects reuse approved designs.
Participate in the **architecture review board** and design reviews early.
Track **architectural debt** (legacy systems, exceptions) in the risk register.
Use architecture to show **how the programme delivers the strategy**: current vs target state and roadmap.

blocks.title: Likely question pattern
blocks.text: "What is the PRIMARY benefit of an information security architecture?" Answer: it aligns security controls with business requirements and the enterprise architecture, enabling consistent, cost-effective protection. Not: it lists all security products.

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY benefit of a security architecture aligned to enterprise architecture?
options: It ensures controls consistently support business requirements
It reduces the number of vendors
quiz.explain: Alignment and traceability to business requirements.

quiz.q: In TOGAF's ADM, which phase defines the target technology architecture?
Which SABSA layer captures business requirements and risk?
quiz.explain: The contextual layer is the business view.

quiz.q: In NIST SP 800-207, which component decides whether access is granted?
quiz.explain: The policy engine makes the decision; the PEP enforces it.

quiz.q: What is the BEST way for security to influence new system designs?
options: Participate in the architecture review board and set security principles early

chapters.title: Domain 4A: Incident management readiness
chapters.summary: Incident response plan, BIA, BCP, DRP, classification, and training, testing and evaluation.

blocks.text: The broader capability (people, process, technology, governance) to prepare for, detect, respond to and learn from incidents.
The operational actions taken when an incident occurs.

An event is any observable occurrence. An incident is an event that harms or threatens the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or systems, or violates policy, and meets defined criteria.
Plan components

items: Purpose, scope and authority (approved by senior management).
Definitions, classification and severity levels.
Roles and responsibilities, including the incident manager and deputies.
Escalation paths and decision authority (e.g. who may shut down a system or pay a ransom).
Procedures and playbooks for common scenarios (ransomware, data breach, business email compromise, DDoS).
Internal and external communication plans, including regulators and law enforcement.
Evidence handling and legal considerations.
Links to BCP and DRP, and criteria for invoking them.
Testing, training and maintenance schedule.

blocks.text: Lifecycle models

rows: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity
Reorganised around NIST CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect (preparation) and Detect, Respond, Recover (response)
Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons learned
Plan and prepare; detection and reporting; assessment and decision; responses; lessons learned

blocks.text: Team models

rows: One team for the organisation; smaller or centralised organisations
Teams per region or business unit with coordination; large or global organisations
Advises and coordinates other teams without direct authority
Retainer with an incident response firm or MSSP; keep an internal owner

blocks.title: Alignment is tested
blocks.text: The incident response plan must align with the BCP and DRP. A question about conflicting plans usually wants them integrated and tested together.
The BIA identifies critical business processes, the impact of disrupting them over time, and the resources they depend on. It drives recovery priorities and objectives.

items: Identify business processes and their owners.
Assess impact over time (financial, customer, regulatory, reputational, safety).
Identify dependencies: people, systems, data, suppliers, facilities.
Set recovery objectives with business owners.
Prioritise recovery.

rows: The target time within which a process or system must be restored after disruption
The maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time before the disruption (drives backup frequency)
Maximum tolerable (period of) downtime: the point beyond which the disruption threatens the organisation's viability or objectives. RTO must be shorter
ISACA term: the maximum period systems can be unavailable before business objectives are compromised
ISACA term: the level of service to be reached during alternate processing until normal service is restored
ISACA term: the maximum time the organisation can operate in alternate process mode

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A payments process loses $200,000 per hour and breaches regulation after 4 hours. The business sets an RTO of 2 hours and an RPO of 5 minutes, which requires real-time replication and a hot site.

blocks.title: Who sets RTO and RPO?
blocks.text: Business process owners set recovery objectives based on the BIA; IT designs solutions to meet them. The lower the RTO and RPO, the higher the cost.
The BCP keeps critical business processes running (possibly in a degraded mode) during and after a disruption. Business continuity management is often run under ISO 22301.

items: Scope and objectives from the BIA.
Continuity strategies for people, premises, technology, information and suppliers.
Crisis management structure and activation criteria.
Manual workarounds and alternate processes.
Communication plans for staff, customers, regulators and media.
Return-to-normal procedures.

blocks.title: BCP vs DRP
blocks.text: The BCP keeps the **business** running; the DRP restores **IT systems and data**. The DRP is one part of the overall continuity capability.

rows: Fully equipped with hardware, software, network; data needs loading or sync
Low, but hard to enforce and test
Changes since the last backup of any type
Needs the last full plus every incremental
Changes since the last full backup
Needs the last full plus the latest differential

blocks.title: Match site to RTO
blocks.text: A short RTO needs a hot or mirrored site; a long RTO tolerates warm or cold. Choosing a more expensive site than the RTO requires isn't cost-effective.

items: **Category** by type: malware, unauthorised access, data breach, denial of service, insider misuse, loss or theft.
**Severity** by business impact: data sensitivity, number of people affected, criticality of systems, regulatory implications, financial impact.
**Priority** combines severity and urgency and drives response time and escalation.
Define clear **thresholds** that trigger escalation to executives, legal, regulators and the crisis team.

rows: Critical service down, confirmed breach of sensitive data, ransomware spreading
Immediate: CISO, executives, crisis team, legal
Contained compromise of a sensitive system; significant data at risk
Isolated policy violation, no data impact

blocks.title: Why classify?
blocks.text: Classification ensures the response is proportionate and the right people are involved at the right time. The PRIMARY purpose of severity levels is to prioritise response and escalation.

sections.title: Incident management training, testing and evaluation

rows: Participants review the plan for completeness and accuracy
Team talks through a scenario step by step
Scenario played out with realistic injects, without affecting operations
Recovery site brought up and processes run alongside production
Production is shut down and operations move to the recovery site

items: Test regularly (at least annually) and after significant change.
Define objectives and success criteria before each test.
Involve business owners, not just IT.
Record findings, assign actions and update the plans.
Train the incident team in their roles; run executive exercises for decision-makers.

blocks.title: Which test first?
blocks.text: For a new plan, start with a checklist review or tabletop before more disruptive tests. The BEST test that validates recovery without disrupting operations is usually a simulation or parallel test.

quiz.q: Who should determine the RTO for a business process?
options: The business process owner, based on the BIA

quiz.q: RPO primarily determines...
quiz.explain: RPO is about acceptable data loss.

quiz.q: Which recovery site is MOST appropriate for an RTO of 2 hours?
Which backup approach requires the last full backup and only the latest backup of its type to restore?
Which test is least disruptive?
quiz.explain: A checklist review involves no operations.

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of incident severity levels?
What should drive recovery priorities?

chapters.title: Domain 4B: Incident management operations
chapters.summary: Tools and techniques, investigation and evidence, containment, communications, eradication and recovery, and post-incident review.

rows: Collect and correlate logs; generate alerts
Enrich alerts with context on indicators and actors
Disk and memory imaging, analysis, timeline reconstruction
Track incidents, actions, evidence and communications
Secure channels if email or chat is compromised

items: **Detection sources:** monitoring alerts, user reports, third parties, law enforcement, threat intelligence.
**Triage:** validate the alert, determine scope and severity, assign an owner.
**Metrics:** mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond or contain, mean time to recover.
**Preserve evidence before changing systems** where possible; involve legal early if prosecution, regulatory action or litigation is possible.
**Chain of custody:** document who collected, handled and stored each item, when and how.
**Forensic soundness:** work on verified copies (images) using write blockers; hash originals and copies.
**Order of volatility:** collect the most volatile data first (CPU registers and cache, memory, network connections and running processes, temporary files, disk, remote logs, archival media).
**Legal hold:** suspend deletion of relevant data when litigation is expected.
**Determine scope and impact:** what systems, data and people are affected, and for how long.

blocks.title: Evidence first
blocks.text: If an incident might lead to legal action, the priority before remediation steps that alter systems is to preserve evidence and maintain chain of custody, unless doing so would cause unacceptable harm.

rows: EDR network isolation of infected endpoints
Block traffic between compromised and clean zones
Disable compromised accounts; revoke tokens and sessions
Block malicious IPs, domains and hashes
Shut down an exposed application temporarily

items: Containment strategies should be **pre-approved** in playbooks, including who can authorise business-impacting actions.
Balance containment against evidence preservation and business impact.
Short-term containment (stop spread now) can be followed by long-term containment (temporary fixes while preparing eradication).

blocks.title: Containment vs business
blocks.text: Shutting down a critical system is a business decision. The security manager recommends; the authority defined in the plan (often the business owner or crisis team) decides.

rows: Timely, factual briefings on impact and decisions needed
Legal notification deadlines (e.g. GDPR requires notifying the authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a qualifying personal data breach); sector-specific rules
Decide with legal counsel and management; may affect evidence handling
Clear, honest notification as law requires; guidance on what they should do
What to say and not say; where to direct inquiries
Contractual notification obligations; insurer approval of vendors and costs

items: **Escalation** follows the thresholds in the plan.
**One source of truth:** a communications lead coordinates messages.
**Legal review** of external statements.
**Out-of-band channels** if corporate systems are compromised.

blocks.title: Who speaks to the media?
blocks.text: Only designated spokespersons (usually corporate communications), with legal review. The security team should not speak to the media directly.

items: **Eradication:** remove malware, persistence mechanisms and attacker access; close the entry point (patch, fix configuration); reset credentials.
**Recovery:** restore from known-good backups or rebuild; validate integrity; return to production in stages.
**Heightened monitoring** after recovery to detect re-infection.
**Business sign-off** that services are working correctly.
**Invoke the DRP or BCP** if recovery exceeds normal capability or RTOs are at risk.

blocks.title: Don't restore the attacker
blocks.text: Restoring backups taken after the initial compromise can restore the attacker's access too. Identify the intrusion date first and restore from before it, or rebuild.

items: Hold a **blameless** review soon after the incident while details are fresh.
Reconstruct the **timeline**: what happened, when detected, how responded.
Identify **root causes** (technical, process and people) using techniques such as the 5 whys or fishbone diagrams.
Record **lessons learned**: what worked, what didn't.
Assign **corrective actions** with owners and dates; track to closure.
**Reassess risk** and update the risk register, plans, playbooks and training.
Report outcomes to senior management.

blocks.title: The PRIMARY purpose
blocks.text: The PRIMARY purpose of a post-incident review is to improve the organisation's response and prevent recurrence, not to assign blame.

quiz.q: An incident may lead to prosecution. What should be ensured FIRST?
options: Evidence is preserved and chain of custody maintained

quiz.q: Which data should be collected FIRST in a forensic investigation?
quiz.explain: Collect the most volatile data first.

quiz.q: Who should authorise shutting down a revenue-critical system during an incident?
options: The authority defined in the incident plan, typically the business owner or crisis team

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a post-incident review?
Why should backups be checked before restoring after ransomware?
options: They may contain malware or the attacker's persistence

quiz.q: Who should speak to the media about a breach?

chapters.title: Final review
chapters.summary: One-page summaries of each domain, key formulas and terms, common traps, and last-week preparation.

rows: Security serves business objectives; senior management is accountable
Six outcomes, roles, strategy inputs, business cases, policies
Manage risk to acceptable levels as defined by appetite; owners decide
Risk terms, ALE, treatment options, ownership, KRIs, reassessment triggers
Deliver the strategy through resources, controls, metrics and third-party management
Classification, policies and exceptions, metrics, control testing, awareness, contracts
Prepare, detect, respond, recover and learn, aligned with BCP and DRP
BIA terms, recovery sites, test types, evidence, communication, post-incident review
Architecture aligns and governs controls across the enterprise
EA and security architecture frameworks, principles, zero trust
ALE before - ALE after - annual control cost
Maximum acceptable data loss in time
Maximum tolerable downtime; RTO must be less
Goal achieved / process performance / risk exposure
Since last backup vs since last full

items: Choosing the technical fix instead of the governance or risk-based answer.
Letting the security manager accept risk (it's the owner's decision).
Thinking risk transfer removes accountability.
Acting before assessing (FIRST questions).
Reporting technical metrics to the board.
Changing policy when a standard or procedure should change.
Skipping the incident plan in the heat of an incident.
Treating compliance as the end goal instead of the minimum.

sections.title: The last week before the exam

items: Do one full timed practice set (150 questions in 4 hours) to test pacing: about 1.6 minutes per question.
Review wrong answers by theme, not by question.
Re-read the mindset chapter and the traps list.
Check exam logistics: ID, test centre or remote proctoring setup, room rules.
Sleep well the night before. Judgement questions suffer more from fatigue than recall questions.

blocks.title: On the day
blocks.text: Flag hard questions and move on. Many candidates run short of time on the last 30 questions. First instinct is often right when you applied the manager mindset.

chapters.title: Practice exam
chapters.summary: 30 scenario questions across all four domains, weighted like the real exam.

sections.title: How to use the practice exam

blocks.text: The quiz for this chapter has 30 scenario questions spread across all four domains, running in order from governance through risk and programme to incident management.

items: Time yourself: about 48 minutes (1.6 minutes per question).
Apply the method from the mindset chapter.
Aim for 24 or more (80%). Review every explanation, including for correct answers.
Retake after a week. Scores that rise because you understand the reasoning, not because you remember the answers, are what matter.

quiz.q: The board asks for assurance that information security supports the company's growth strategy. What should the security manager provide FIRST?
options: A mapping of the security strategy to business objectives
quiz.explain: Strategic alignment is shown by tracing security strategy to business objectives.

quiz.q: Which is the MOST important factor in determining the level of protection for an information asset?
options: Its classification based on business value and sensitivity
quiz.explain: Protection is proportionate to value and sensitivity.

quiz.q: A new CISO finds security policies that haven't been updated in five years. What should be done FIRST?
options: Review them against current business objectives, risks and regulations

quiz.q: Which is the BEST indicator of senior management commitment to security?
options: Approval and funding of the security strategy and active participation in the steering committee
quiz.explain: Commitment shows in approval, funding and involvement.

quiz.q: An organisation operating in several countries finds conflicting data retention laws. What should the security manager do?
options: Escalate to legal and senior management to decide a compliant approach
quiz.explain: Legal interpretation and risk decisions belong to legal and management.

quiz.q: A risk assessment shows a risk above appetite, but the business owner refuses to fund mitigation. What should the security manager do?
options: Escalate to senior management for a decision
Accept the risk on the owner's behalf

quiz.q: What is the MAIN reason to perform risk assessments periodically?
options: Threats, vulnerabilities and business context change

quiz.q: A vulnerability affects a system whose owner accepts the risk. What must be ensured?
options: The acceptance is documented, within appetite and approved by someone with authority
quiz.explain: Formal acceptance keeps risk visible and accountable.

quiz.q: Which factor MOST influences the choice of risk treatment?
options: Cost of treatment compared with risk reduction and appetite

quiz.q: A third party will process customer data. When should security requirements be defined?
What is the BEST way to measure the effectiveness of a security programme?
options: Metrics showing progress against objectives and risk reduction

quiz.q: Security staff spend most time on low-value tasks. What is the BEST first step?
options: Analyse processes and prioritise based on risk and objectives

quiz.q: Which is the PRIMARY objective of an information security awareness programme?
A developer requests an exception to the encryption standard for a legacy app. Who should approve it?
options: The risk owner, after a risk assessment and with compensating controls
quiz.explain: Owners approve exceptions based on risk.

quiz.q: Which control type is a warning banner on a login page?
An internal audit finds that access reviews aren't performed. Who should own the remediation?
options: The control owner responsible for access reviews

quiz.q: What is the BEST way to ensure security is considered in new projects?
options: Integrate security requirements into the project methodology from initiation

quiz.q: Which is the MOST important element when outsourcing security monitoring to an MSSP?
